A lot of people ask how I broke into AI research as an undergrad at Kathmandu University. My playbook:

Build in public. I shipped 'Smart NID Helper' to solve a real local problem (Nepal NID forms) and documented the whole process. Don't just research; deploy.

What are you currently building?

Low-resource NLP doesn't get enough attention, but it's where the real impact is.

For our CHiPSAL 2026 paper, we used a Random Forest reward model to filter 68 hours of noisy Nepali speech, cutting Whisper's WER by 11%.

You don't always need more compute. Sometimes you just need cleaner data.

My biggest realization as the AI Lead at Kurly Brains:

Clients don't care about the size of your LLM. They care if the WordPress chatbot actually answers their customer's specific question without hallucinating.

Stop chasing model sizes. Start chasing pipeline reliability.

The "Prompting Is Not Adaptation" paper we submitted to ICON 2026 taught me a hard lesson.

When evaluating audio-language models for Nepali ASR, prompting them just couldn't match true language adaptation. 

Fine-tuning is still king for low-resource languages. Don't let the zero-shot hype fool you.

Building an end-to-end ML system is 80% data and deployment, 20% modeling.

When I built the Drone Image Landcover Segmentation pipeline, training DeepLab v3 in PyTorch was the easiest part. GIS preprocessing? Absolute nightmare.

Learn the plumbing, not just the math.

Accessibility tech is why I love computer vision.

I built a real-time Webcam Eye-Tracking system using MediaPipe and Ridge Regression so users with severe motor disabilities can control their OS hands-free.

Tech at its best empowers people. What problem are you solving?
